Key observations:
- Field-level view showing mostly dead/dried soybean plants in the background, with one green plant standing out in the foreground
- The background plants are completely brown and desiccated, with dried pods and leaves — premature death
- The foreground plant has green leaves and green stem, appearing healthy relative to the dead surrounding plants
- This is a classic "green stem disorder" pattern — stems remain green while the rest of the plant/field has matured and died, or one plant stays green while surrounding plants are dead

The contrast between the one green-stemmed plant and the completely dried/dead field plants is the hallmark of **Green Stem Disorder** in soybean, where affected plants retain green stems and leaves past normal maturity while surrounding plants have senesced. Wait — actually, looking again, the green plant in the foreground appears normal/healthy while the background plants are all dead/diseased. This could also be **Sudden Death Syndrome** causing premature defoliation and death of the field plants.

However, the most prominent feature is the entire field of prematurely dead/dried plants with one surviving green plant — this pattern of field-wide premature death with foliar death but retained structure is more consistent with **Sudden Death Syndrome** (SDS), which causes premature death with retained dried foliage and pods on standing dead plants.
